entries.speaker: David Hilbert
entries.quote:
Wir dürfen nicht denen glauben, die heute mit philosophischer Miene und überlegenem Tone den Kulturuntergang prophezeien und sich in dem Ignorabimus gefallen. Für uns gibt es kein Ignorabimus, und meiner Meinung nach auch für die Naturwissenschaft überhaupt nicht. Statt des törichten Ignorabimus heiße im Gegenteil unsere Lösung:
Wir müssen wissen,
Wir werden wissen.
entries.work: quoted in James T. Smith, “Hilbert’s 1930 Radio Address” (San Francisco State University, 4 September 2004), German transcription of the radio excerpt of Naturerkennen und Logik, address to the Gesellschaft Deutscher Naturforscher und Ärzte, Königsberg (radio excerpt)

entries.speaker: David Hilbert
entries.quote:
We must not believe those, who today with philosophical bearing and deliberative tone prophesy the fall of culture and accept the ignorabimus. For us there is no ignorabimus, and in my opinion none whatever in natural science. In opposition to the foolish ignorabimus I offer our answer:
We must know,
We will know.
entries.work: quoted in James T. Smith, “Hilbert’s 1930 Radio Address” (San Francisco State University, 4 September 2004), English translation by James T. Smith of the radio excerpt of Naturerkennen und Logik, address to the Gesellschaft Deutscher Naturforscher und Ärzte, Königsberg (radio excerpt)

entries.speaker: David Hilbert
entries.quote: This conviction of the solvability of every mathematical problem is a powerful incentive to the worker. We hear within us the perpetual call: There is the problem. Seek its solution. You can find it by pure reason, for in mathematics there is no ignorabimus.
entries.work: “Mathematical Problems,” lecture to the International Congress of Mathematicians, Paris, 1900; trans. Mary Winton Newson, Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 8 (1902), pp. 437–479

entries.speaker: David Hilbert
entries.quote: An example of the kind of fundamental questions which can be so handled is the thesis that every mathematical problem is solvable. We are all convinced that it really is so. In fact one of the principal attractions of tackling a mathematical problem is that we always hear this cry within us: There is the problem, find the answer; you can find it just by thinking, for there is no ignorabimus in mathematics.
entries.work: “On the infinite” (“Über das Unendliche,” Mathematische Annalen 95 (1926), pp. 161–190), lecture delivered 4 June 1925 to the Westphalian Mathematical Society, Münster; trans. Erna Putnam and Gerald J. Massey, in Paul Benacerraf and Hilary Putnam (eds.), Philosophy of Mathematics: Selected Readings (Cambridge University Press), pp. 183–201
